items.definition: A situation where two people hold different views and are still talking. The other person is not automatically an enemy.
items.example: It was a disagreement about the schedule, not a fight.

items.definition: A disagreement that improves the decision being made and leaves the working relationship intact.
items.example: The meeting was tense but productive — it ended with a constructive disagreement and a clear next step.

items.definition: Soft words that mark your opinion as your opinion, such as 'maybe' or 'I could be wrong'. Useful in small doses.
items.example: A little hedging language keeps a sentence civil; too much of it hides your point.

items.definition: Giving the other side's position its strongest and most honest form before you argue against it.
items.example: Before you answer, steelman the other view in one sentence and see if it still convinces you.

items.definition: The part of a position that both people accept. Every polite disagreement starts by naming it.
items.example: Find the common ground first — both of you want this project to succeed.

items.definition: Listening to understand the other person's point, including checking your understanding, instead of waiting for your turn to speak.
items.example: Active listening means repeating their concern back before you answer it.

items.definition: Short, friendly conversation with someone you do not know well. Its purpose is contact, not important information.
items.example: We had some small talk about the rain and ended up talking for an hour.

items.definition: The first thing you say to start a conversation. It should be easy for the other person to answer.
items.example: My usual opener at a party is a question about what brought them there.

items.definition: A question that cannot be answered with one word and that gives the other person room to talk.
items.example: What made you take that job?

items.definition: A question built on what the other person just said, which shows you were listening.
items.example: You said you moved last year — what was it like at first?

items.definition: A short sound or remark that shows you are following without taking the turn, such as 'mm' or 'really'.
items.example: You say 'really?' and then let them keep going.

items.definition: A prepared sentence that ends a conversation politely while leaving the door open for another meeting.
items.example: It was really nice meeting you — see you around.

items.definition: A comfortable relationship between people, built when each can predict how the other will behave.
items.example: We had no topic in common, but we talked for twenty minutes and had instant rapport.

items.definition: The length of time you can hold focus on one task. It depends on the task and on your state, not on a fixed personal rating.
items.example: My attention span on a spreadsheet is fine; it is the phone that breaks it.

items.definition: The part of the previous task still in your head after you stop it, which lowers the quality of the next task.
items.example: I checked messages between every paragraph, so both pieces of work suffered.

items.definition: A reward schedule where the outcome is unpredictable. Unpredictable rewards keep a behaviour going far longer than predictable ones.
items.example: You keep opening the app because you never know which post will be interesting.

items.definition: A brain chemical linked to reward and motivation. People say it loosely; the useful idea is that wanting and liking are different things.
items.example: The video was not even good, but the pull to check again was strong.

items.definition: Reading bad news repeatedly on purpose, because the subject holds your attention. A specific habit, not a synonym for scrolling.
items.example: That was an hour of doomscrolling, and I felt worse each time I checked.

items.definition: The habit of ignoring alerts on purpose, so that the one alert that mattered gets ignored too.
items.example: I turned off all notifications, and now nothing gets through, including the messages from my family.

items.definition: A fraudulent message, usually by email, designed to steal credentials or money by pretending to be someone you trust.
items.example: That email about a locked account was phishing, and it used our bank's real logo.

items.definition: Phishing carried out by text message. Short, urgent, and arriving on the phone you are holding.
items.example: The message about a parcel was smishing, and the link was not the courier's website.

items.definition: Phishing carried out by a phone call, usually with a claim of authority from a bank, a police force or a support line.
items.example: They called pretending to be the tax office. That is vishing, and I hung up and called the real number.

items.definition: Presenting a false sender identity so that a call or a message appears to come from a number or address that belongs to someone else.
items.example: The message showed my brother's name, but the number was spoofed.

items.definition: The short number a bank sends to confirm a login or a payment. Anyone who holds it can complete the action.
items.example: I gave them the one-time code, and that was the moment the account was theirs.

items.definition: A bank account used to receive and pass on criminal money, sometimes opened by someone who believes they are helping a company or a cause.
items.example: They asked me to receive money and pass it on. That makes my account a mule account and the money is stolen.

items.definition: A reversal of a card payment requested from the bank, usually because the transaction was not authorised or the goods never arrived.
items.example: The bank raised a chargeback and returned the money five days later.

items.definition: Money demanded before a service is delivered. Common in fake job offers, fake investments and fake love interests.
items.example: They wanted a small fee before the equipment arrived, and then a larger one.

items.definition: The moment you take the room, normally from 14:00 or 15:00. Before it, the hotel usually stores your luggage free of charge.
items.example: Check-in is from 14:00, but I can leave my bags with you in the morning.

items.definition: The card or fob that opens your door. In many hotels it also works as your room number, your lift pass and your breakfast voucher.
items.example: Could I have a second key card for my colleague?

items.definition: A sum held on your card, or taken in cash, to cover extras and damage. It is released after you leave.
items.example: We hold a deposit of 200 on your card for the minibar and the safe.

items.definition: Giving the room back and paying the final bill, usually between 10:00 and 12:00. Late check-out can often be arranged.
items.example: Can I check out at 14:00 instead of 11:00? My flight is at 17:00.

items.definition: Free storage of bags before check-in or after check-out, which lets you use the city without carrying a suitcase.
items.example: Could you store my luggage until my flight in the evening?

items.definition: The team that cleans the rooms, changes the linen and takes away used towels.
items.example: Could housekeeping bring two more towels, please?

items.definition: The staff member who arranges tickets, tours, taxis, doctors and anything else the hotel does not sell itself.
items.example: The concierge booked a table at a restaurant that was fully booked.

items.definition: A temporary fix that makes a problem go away without solving it.
items.example: We applied a band-aid to the payment process, but the real fix is in the accounting system.

items.definition: A way of working around a problem instead of fixing its cause.
items.example: The manual workaround is for us to check the total by hand every Friday.

items.definition: To return to a topic later. Often used to postpone a decision.
items.example: Let us circle back to the budget question after lunch.

items.definition: To have a short conversation with someone about something.
items.example: Can we touch base on Thursday for fifteen minutes?

items.definition: To move a discussion out of the meeting into a smaller group.
items.example: Let us take this offline and I will send you the figures.

items.definition: To raise an issue or a risk so that people notice it early.
items.example: I want to flag a risk in the schedule before it becomes a problem.
